title: Tug of War
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore tug of war as a simple, ancient game: its rules as played in modern competition (Tug of War International Federation rules, two-pull matches, four-meter sidelines, anchor's rope wrap, natural-fiber rope, footwear), its history from Viking and Nordic contests and British Navy use to the Korean Jeju Daerigi festival, Okinawa's rope festival, India's rassakashi, and its brief run at the 1900–1920 Olympics where police teams swept the 1908 podium. They cover the TWIF's founding in 1960, eighties TV tug of war (Battle of the Network Stars, Superstars), the dangers of rope snaps and looped ropes, and the Squid Game tug of war scene. The episode closes with a listener mail item about a red-tailed hawk standing in for an eagle cry, and a note from producer Katie Rose about the board game restock.

segments.title: Opening banter and eighties tug of war memories
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce part two of the rudimentary games series, reminisce about tug of war on eighties TV such as Superstars and Battle of the Network Stars, and mention Squid Game and childhood field day games.

segments.title: What tug of war is
segments.summary: The hosts define tug of war as a game where two opposing sides pull on a rope to drag the other past a center line or make them let go, and describe how it is played in school gyms and on TV.

segments.title: Ancient and global history of tug of war
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the game's worldwide spread across millennia, including Viking and Nordic sports, the British Navy using it to settle a propeller versus paddle wheel debate, and its use as a way to settle disputes.

segments.title: Tug of war traditions in India, Korea, Japan and the Americas
segments.summary: The hosts describe rassakashi in India, a depiction at the Konark Sun Temple, the Jeju Daerigi festival in Korea with its very large rope, and Okinawa's festival that reportedly set a world record for attendance and participation. They also discuss possible Indigenous American and colonial origins.

segments.title: Ancient Olympic claims and the 1900 to 1920 Olympic run
segments.summary: The hosts say claims that tug of war was an ancient Olympic event lack evidence. They describe its Olympic run in the early 1900s, club teams, the 1908 Olympics where British police teams took the podium, and its removal after 1920.

segments.title: Olympic mistaken identity and the TWIF founding
segments.summary: The hosts correct a popular claim that Constantine Enriquez was the first Black Olympian to win a tug of war medal, noting Francisco Enriquez won the silver in tug of war. They discuss the IOC recognizing the TWIF and the founding of the Tug of War International Federation in 1960 by George Hutton with the Swedes.
topics: Tug of War International Federation founding

segments.title: Competition weight classes, rope and anchor rules, and footwear
segments.summary: The hosts cover matching team weight classes, eight-person international teams, the natural-fiber rope and its dimensions, anchor rope wrap, palms-up grip rule, the driver's role, and footwear and boots that aid leg-driven pulling power.

segments.title: How a tug of war match is run and scored
segments.summary: The hosts describe a match: taking up the rope, centering it, the four-meter sideline marks, the judge's commands, two-out-of-three pulls, the no-pull call and disqualification, and that competitive leagues still run.

segments.title: Tug of War dangers, rope snaps, and Squid Game strategy
segments.summary: The hosts warn about amputations and deaths from rope snaps, looped ropes, and synthetic rope stretch. They discuss the Squid Game tug of war scene, its strategy, and a study that tested it, plus the show's season two.
topics: Squid Game tug of war strategy

segments.title: Listener mail: eagle versus hawk cry and board game restock
segments.summary: A listener notes that the eagle cry in the Cookies episode is a red-tailed hawk call, which Hollywood uses instead. Producer Katie Rose asks about the board game, and the hosts say it sold out but should restock in January.
